scope.selection: Four documented federal procurement, railroad-finance, appointment and resource-lease cases; illustrative, not an exhaustive ranking.
scope.status: Private research input; no publication performed.
scope.currency_basis: Historical nominal US dollars; no inflation conversion.
scope.source_method: Primary judicial opinions, statute and original congressional findings/charges reproduced in official records; institutional compilations identified explicitly.

cases.title: Providence Tool: contingent compensation for a federal musket contract

amounts.status: Norris's claimed compensation; company disputed the amount; payment not established.
Trial judgment for Norris, subsequently reversed; not a verified disbursement.

cases.policy_instrument: July 1861 War Department contract: 25,000 muskets at US$20 each.

public_contract_value.status: Calculated contract face value: 25,000 × 20; not verified spending.

cases.established_connection: The Court's record attributes procurement to Norris's efforts under a contingent agreement and describes influential introductions to Secretary of War Simon Cameron.
cases.outcome: In 1864 the Supreme Court held the compensation agreement unenforceable on public-policy grounds and remanded for a new trial.
cases.counterevidence_and_limits: The rule rested on the agreement's tendency, without requiring proof of improper means. This is neither a proved bribe to Cameron nor proof that the musket contract itself was canceled.
cases.documented_roles: Company: Rhode Island corporation supplying arms. Norris: intermediary. Cameron: Secretary of War.

sources.title: Tool Company v. Norris, 69 U.S. (2 Wall.) 45 (1864)
sources.locator: Statement of facts, pp.45–48; opinion, pp.53–56.
sources.source_type: Primary Supreme Court opinion and case statement, reproduced by Justia.

cases.title: Crédit Mobilier: benefits to James Brooks within a subsidized railroad enterprise
cases.payer: Thomas C. Durant / Crédit Mobilier; later issuance arranged through Sidney Dillon
cases.recipient: Charles H. Neilson, named holder; House committee found James Brooks the beneficial owner
cases.money_type: Discounted securities purchase and associated benefits; distinct from public railroad financing

amounts.status: Brooks paid for 100 Crédit Mobilier shares transferred December 26, 1867.
Union Pacific bonds accompanying that transaction; stated securities amount, not cash.
Union Pacific stock accompanying that transaction; stated securities amount, not market value.
Price of 50 additional shares issued to Neilson February 29, 1868; financed by Dillon. Committee described their value as US$15,000–20,000; repayment unresolved.

cases.established_connection: The committee found the additional shares secured Brooks's official favor. Brooks and Alley denied the alleged promise to influence the Democratic side; the committee relied on surrounding circumstances too.
cases.documented_roles: Brooks: Representative and government director of Union Pacific; Dillon: Crédit Mobilier president.
cases.policy_instrument: Pacific Railroad Act, July 1, 1862, §§1, 5–6: Union Pacific charter and repayable federal bond aid.

public_financing.status: Base statutory bond-aid authorization; not a corporate political payment or verified total disbursement.

cases.outcome: February 27, 1873: House censured Ames and Brooks; Brooks vote 174–32. The adopted resolution condemned use of his offices to obtain stock.
cases.counterevidence_and_limits: The committee did not find corrupt intent in the other previously discussed House purchasers. Later share transactions cannot establish that they caused the earlier 1862 statute; no specific subsequent roll-call purchased by Brooks's benefits is identified here.

sources.title: Congressional Globe, February 18, 1873: Poland committee report
sources.locator: Printed p.1464: opening findings and 'James Brooks, of New York' passage.
sources.source_type: Original congressional investigation report, archived by University of North Texas; OCR available.

cases.title: Fort Sill trading appointment: Evans–Marsh–Belknap payments
cases.payer: John S. Evans → Caleb P. Marsh → William W. Belknap
cases.recipient: Marsh, intermediary; Belknap, Secretary of War
cases.money_type: Contracted intermediary payments and alleged official kickbacks

amounts.status: October 8, 1870 Evans–Marsh contract, payable quarterly; later terms could change.
Receipt by Belknap on or about November 2, 1870, alleged in Article IV, specification 1.

cases.policy_instrument: Appointment of Evans as Fort Sill post trader on October 10, 1870, and continued tenure.
cases.established_connection: House articles expressly tied payments to appointment and retention; Article III alleged Marsh passed half to Belknap.
cases.outcome: August 1, 1876: Senate acquitted on every article because no guilty vote reached two-thirds.
cases.counterevidence_and_limits: Charges are not a conviction. The official compilation records 22 not-guilty votes based on jurisdiction and three on evidence. Annual rates changed; no extrapolated multi-year total is asserted. This concerns administrative patronage, not proof of purchasing a statute.
cases.documented_roles: Evans: trader; Marsh: intermediary; Belknap: Secretary of War.

sources.title: Hinds' Precedents, Volume 3, Chapter 77: Impeachment and Trial of William W. Belknap
sources.locator: §2449, Articles I, III, IV specification 1 and V; §2467, final votes and acquittal.
sources.source_type: Official reproduction of impeachment articles and Senate disposition; charges and verdict distinguished.

cases.title: Doheny–Fall: US$100,000 and Elk Hills oil leases
cases.payer: Edward L. Doheny, through his son
cases.recipient: Albert B. Fall, Secretary of the Interior
cases.money_type: Cash advance described as a loan; corrupt influence judicially established in civil litigation

amounts.status: Delivered November 30, 1921; demand note given; no principal or interest repayment reported in the opinion.

cases.policy_instrument: Pan American contracts of April 25 and December 11, 1922; Naval Petroleum Reserve No.1 leases of June 5 and December 11, 1922.
cases.established_connection: The Supreme Court sustained findings that Doheny corruptly secured Fall's influence and official action; Fall collusively dominated negotiations.
cases.outcome: February 28, 1927: cancellation upheld; contracts and leases held illegal and void.
cases.counterevidence_and_limits: Companies argued loan, not bribe. Civil rescission did not require statutory criminal bribery or government financial loss. This opinion is not a criminal conviction of Doheny. Elk Hills is the California transaction, not Sinclair's Wyoming Teapot Dome lease.
cases.documented_roles: Doheny controlled the two Pan American companies and served as Petroleum Company's president, then board chairman.

sources.title: Pan American Petroleum & Transport Co. v. United States, 273 U.S.456 (1927)
sources.locator: pp.485–486 (instruments); pp.493–494 (payment); pp.498–500 (findings and limits); pp.500–503 (authority and disposition).
sources.source_type: Primary Supreme Court opinion, reproduced by FindLaw.

continuity_review.supported: Recurring mechanisms include contingent access fees, preferential securities, appointment payments and corruption of administrative contracting. USW04's opinion at p.500 expressly cites Tool Company v. Norris: a documented legal-doctrine link.
continuity_review.not_established: These cases do not prove continuity of a single family, organization, fund, motive or control structure into modern institutions.
continuity_review.slavery_or_forced_labor: No selected source establishes such a link for these particular transactions. That connection remains unestablished in this bounded review, not disproved. Official and business roles are recorded without ancestry-based guilt or inferred personal motive.
continuity_review.forward_backward_check: Payment promises, actual transfers, allegations and adjudicated findings are separated. Later benefits are not used to explain earlier legislation; invalidation, denial and acquittal remain attached to their cases.

notes: Six distinct primary-source URLs support four cases. The Hinds compilations reproduce source proceedings; their later editorial dates are not event dates.
Security face amounts, purchase prices, estimated market values and public financing are not added together.
The Norris fee case was selected over less securely sourced aggregate claims about the 1896 or 1904 elections.
No general First World War narrative was repeated. No new conclusion about modern companies is inferred from these historical cases.
An additive input save is authorized; independent destination readback and package preservation remain the coordinator's next step.
